records.source: Γνωρίζω δὲ ὑμῖν, ἀδελφοί, τὸ εὐαγγέλιον ὃ εὐηγγελισάμην ὑμῖν, ὃ καὶ παρελάβετε, ἐν ᾧ καὶ ἑστήκατε, δι’ οὗ καὶ σῴζεσθε, τίνι λόγῳ εὐηγγελισάμην ὑμῖν, εἰ κατέχετε, ἐκτὸς εἰ μὴ εἰκῇ ἐπιστεύσατε.
records.gloss: I make known but to you, brothers, the gospel which I proclaimed to you, which also you received, in which also you stand, \v 2 through which also you are being saved, with what word I proclaimed [it] to you, if you hold fast, unless in vain you believed.
pieces: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, I am setting out for you once more the gospel I proclaimed to you. You received it, you stand firm in it,
and through it you are being saved, if you keep hold of the message as I proclaimed it to you. Otherwise you came to believe for nothing.

L.1: Now I make known to you, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, the gospel that I proclaimed to you, which you also received, in which you also stand,
L.2: through which you are also being saved, with what message I proclaimed [it] to you, if you are holding [it] fast, unless you believed in vain.

R.1: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, let me remind you of the good news I told you. You accepted it, and you are standing firm in it.
R.2: Through it God is saving you, as long as you hold on to the message just as I told it to you. If you do not, your believing was for nothing.

decisions.choice: I make known: here, I set out again what they already know, as the ground for the argument that follows
decisions.reason: Γνωρίζω usually means to make something known, but the Corinthians have already received this gospel and stand in it (verses 1-2). Paul restates it so that he can build on it in verses 12-34.

decisions.choice: are being saved: salvation as something under way, to be completed at the end
alternatives: are saved, as a finished state
decisions.reason: σῴζεσθε is present tense, as in 1:18 ("us who are being saved"). The salvation that began when they believed reaches its goal at the resurrection, the subject of this chapter.

decisions.choice: if you hold fast: the condition is that they keep hold of the message in the form in which Paul proclaimed it
alternatives: "I make known ... in what words I proclaimed it", taking the phrase with the opening verb
decisions.reason: The order of τίνι λόγῳ εὐηγγελισάμην ὑμῖν εἰ κατέχετε is unusual, with the question word placed before the condition. Read with κατέχετε ("you hold fast"), it says what they must keep hold of: the gospel as Paul put it to them, which he now repeats in verses 3-5.

decisions.choice: in vain: to no purpose, a faith that would come to nothing
decisions.reason: εἰκῇ can mean either. Verses 14 and 17 show what Paul has in mind: faith would be empty and futile if Christ had not been raised. He does not think this is so; the clause sharpens the warning against denying the resurrection.

decisions.choice: I am setting out for you once more
decisions.reason: Balanced shows that Paul is restating what they already know (m1); Readable says "let me remind you".

decisions.choice: God is saving you
decisions.reason: Readable names God as the one who saves, which the passive leaves unstated.

records.heading: The resurrection of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}

records.source: Παρέδωκα γὰρ ὑμῖν ἐν πρώτοις, ὃ καὶ παρέλαβον, ὅτι Χριστὸς ἀπέθανεν ὑπὲρ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν κατὰ τὰς γραφάς, καὶ ὅτι ἐτάφη, καὶ ὅτι ἐγήγερται τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ τρίτῃ κατὰ τὰς γραφάς, καὶ ὅτι ὤφθη Κηφᾷ, εἶτα τοῖς δώδεκα·
records.gloss: I handed on for to you among first [things], what also I received, that Christ died for the sins of us according to the scriptures, \v 4 and that he was buried, and that he has been raised on the day the third according to the scriptures, \v 5 and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve;
pieces: What I handed on to you, as the first and chief thing, I myself had received: that {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} died for our sins, in keeping with the Scriptures;
that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was buried; that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has been raised on the third day, in keeping with the Scriptures;
and that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} appeared to Cephas, and after that to the Twelve.

L.3: For I handed on to you among [the] first things what I also received: that {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} died for our sins according to the Scriptures,
L.4: and that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was buried, and that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has been raised on the third day according to the Scriptures,
L.5: and that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} appeared to Cephas, then to the Twelve.

R.3: I passed on to you the most important message of all, the one that was passed on to me. {{christos:Christ|The Messiah}} died for our sins, just as the Scriptures said would happen.
R.4: He was buried. God raised {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to life on the third day, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is alive, just as the Scriptures said.
R.5: He appeared to Peter, and then to the Twelve, {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} closest followers.

decisions.choice: handed on ... received: the words for passing on a tradition faithfully, from teacher to learner
decisions.reason: Παρέδωκα and παρέλαβον are the pair Paul uses for the Lord's Supper in 11:23 and for the traditions in 11:2, and ὑπὲρ in verse 1 is the Corinthians' side of it. The lines that follow, each beginning with ὅτι ("that"), read like a fixed summary Paul was taught and taught in turn. He also says that his gospel came to him by revelation (Galatians 1:11-12); the two do not conflict, since what he was taught agreed with what the risen Lord showed him.

decisions.choice: among the first things: as of first importance, the heart of the gospel
alternatives: first in time, the first thing I taught you
decisions.reason: ἐν πρώτοις can mean first in order of time or first in importance. Both may be meant: this was where Paul began, and it is what everything else rests on.

decisions.choice: according to the Scriptures: Christ's death for sins and his being raised happened as the Scriptures of Israel said, without one passage being named
decisions.reason: Paul names no text. For a death "for our sins", the clearest candidate is Isaiah 53:4-12, where the servant bears the sins of many. For the raising, Psalm 16:10 is used of Jesus' resurrection in Acts 2:25-31, and some connect "on the third day" with Hosea 6:2 or with Jonah 1:17 (compare Matthew 12:40). It is not certain whether the second phrase goes with "on the third day" or with the raising as a whole.

decisions.choice: has been raised: raised once and still alive
alternatives: was raised, as a past event only
decisions.reason: The other verbs in the list, ἀπέθανεν ("died"), ἐτάφη ("was buried") and ὤφθη ("appeared"), look back on single events. ἐγήγερται alone is a perfect: Christ was raised and lives now. Paul keeps this tense all through verses 12-20. The passive means that God raised him (verse 15).

decisions.choice: was buried: his death was real and complete
decisions.reason: Burial confirms death. The four lines go together in pairs: he died and was buried; he was raised and was seen.

decisions.choice: Cephas is Peter; the Twelve is the name of the group Jesus chose
decisions.reason: Cephas is the Aramaic name Jesus gave Peter (John 1:42), as in 1:12. "The Twelve" was the group's name even when Judas was no longer among them; Luke 24:33 speaks of "the Eleven" at this point.

decisions.choice: follow the SBLGNT: "the Twelve"
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts, mainly Western witnesses, read "the Eleven", which looks like a correction to account for Judas. Reviewers must check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: What I handed on to you ... I myself had received
alternatives: For I handed on to you ... what I also received
decisions.reason: Balanced follows the same pattern as 11:23, putting the teaching they already have first.

decisions.choice: in keeping with the Scriptures
decisions.reason: Balanced says plainly that the events match what the Scriptures say; Literal keeps the traditional form. Readable says "just as the Scriptures said".

decisions.choice: God raised {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to life ... and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is alive; Peter; {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} closest followers
alternatives: has been raised; Cephas; the Twelve
decisions.reason: Readable names God as the one who raised him and spells out the lasting result of the perfect (m4). It uses the name Peter, as the book does at Readable (1:12), and says who the Twelve were.

records.source: ἔπειτα ὤφθη ἐπάνω πεντακοσίοις ἀδελφοῖς ἐφάπαξ, ἐξ ὧν οἱ πλείονες μένουσιν ἕως ἄρτι, τινὲς δὲ ἐκοιμήθησαν·
records.gloss: then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once, of whom the most remain until now, some but fell asleep;
pieces: Next {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} appeared to more than 500 {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}} on a single occasion. Most of them are alive to this day, but some have died.

L.6: Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} appeared to more than 500 {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}} at one time, of whom the greater part remain until now, but some have fallen asleep.

R.6: Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} appeared to more than 500 {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}} at one time. Most of them are still alive today, but some have died.

decisions.choice: brothers: fellow believers, men and women
decisions.reason: ἀδελφοῖς is Paul's usual word for members of the church, women included. Nothing limits this crowd to men, though ancient writers sometimes counted only the men in a crowd (Matthew 14:21).

decisions.choice: remain: are still alive
decisions.reason: Paul's point is that most of these witnesses can still be asked about what they saw.

decisions.choice: fell asleep: died
decisions.reason: ἐκοιμήθησαν is the gentle way of speaking of believers' death used in 7:39 and 11:30, which looks forward to waking at the resurrection, the subject of this chapter (verses 18, 20).

decisions.choice: have died
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the meaning of the idiom (m3), as at 7:39 and 11:30; Literal keeps it.

records.source: ἔπειτα ὤφθη Ἰακώβῳ, εἶτα τοῖς ἀποστόλοις πᾶσιν·
records.gloss: then he appeared to James, then to the apostles all;
pieces: Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} appeared to James, and after him to all the apostles.

L.7: Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} appeared to James, then to all the apostles.

R.7: Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} appeared to James, the Lord's brother, and later to all the apostles.

decisions.choice: James: the brother of the Lord, later a leader of the church in Jerusalem
alternatives: James the son of Zebedee, one of the Twelve
decisions.reason: Paul calls this James "the Lord's brother" (Galatians 1:19) and names him among the pillars of the Jerusalem church (Galatians 2:9). Jesus' brothers did not believe in him during his ministry (John 7:5); an appearance to James helps explain the change. The son of Zebedee was already among the Twelve (verse 5).

decisions.choice: all the apostles: a wider group than the Twelve
decisions.reason: Paul uses "apostle" for more people than the Twelve: James (Galatians 1:19), Barnabas (9:5-6), Andronicus and Junia (Romans 16:7). "All" suggests a larger group than in verse 5, though which people are meant cannot be known.

decisions.choice: James, the Lord's brother
decisions.reason: Readable says which James is meant (m1), from Galatians 1:19.

records.source: ἔσχατον δὲ πάντων ὡσπερεὶ τῷ ἐκτρώματι ὤφθη κἀμοί.
records.gloss: last but of all as if to the untimely birth he appeared also to me.
pieces: Last of all, as though to a child born before its time, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} appeared to me as well.

L.8: And last of all, as if to the untimely birth, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} appeared to me too.

R.8: Finally {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} appeared to me too, though I was like a baby born at the wrong time.

decisions.choice: untimely birth: a child born dead or too early, a picture of Paul's unfitness and of the abrupt, unnatural way he was made an apostle
alternatives: one born late, after the others
a term of abuse his opponents used of him ("freak")
decisions.reason: ἐκτρώματι means a miscarriage or stillborn child; the Greek Old Testament uses it that way (Numbers 12:12; Job 3:16). So the picture is of an unformed, abnormal birth rather than a late one. Verse 9 explains it: Paul was not fit to be an apostle. The article ("the untimely birth") may suggest a label others had used of him, but that cannot be shown.

decisions.choice: last of all: the appearance to Paul was the last of its kind, and of the same kind as the others
decisions.reason: Paul puts the risen Lord's appearance to him (9:1; Acts 9:3-6) in the same list as the appearances to Peter and the others, and at the end of it. This is the ground of his apostleship.

decisions.choice: a child born before its time (B); a baby born at the wrong time (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the picture in everyday words; Literal keeps "untimely birth".

records.source: ἐγὼ γάρ εἰμι ὁ ἐλάχιστος τῶν ἀποστόλων, ὃς οὐκ εἰμὶ ἱκανὸς καλεῖσθαι ἀπόστολος, διότι ἐδίωξα τὴν ἐκκλησίαν τοῦ θεοῦ·
records.gloss: I for am the least of the apostles, who not am fit to be called apostle, because I persecuted the church of the God;
pieces: Among the apostles I am the least; I am not even fit to bear the name apostle, because I persecuted God's church.

L.9: For I am the least of the apostles, who am not fit to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God.

R.9: You see, I am the least important of the apostles. I am not good enough even to be called an apostle, because I used to attack God's church.

decisions.choice: the least: lowest in standing, because of his past
decisions.reason: Paul does not say he did the least work; verse 10 says the opposite. He is least because of what he did before he met the Lord.

decisions.choice: fit: qualified, good enough
decisions.reason: ἱκανὸς means sufficient or qualified, as in 2 Corinthians 2:16 and 3:5-6, where Paul says his fitness comes from God.

decisions.choice: persecuted: Paul hunted down believers before his conversion
decisions.reason: Acts 8:3 and 9:1-2 describe it, and Paul speaks of it in Galatians 1:13 and Philippians 3:6.

decisions.choice: used to attack
decisions.reason: Readable uses a plainer verb and marks it as something in Paul's past.

records.source: χάριτι δὲ θεοῦ εἰμι ὅ εἰμι, καὶ ἡ χάρις αὐτοῦ ἡ εἰς ἐμὲ οὐ κενὴ ἐγενήθη, ἀλλὰ περισσότερον αὐτῶν πάντων ἐκοπίασα, οὐκ ἐγὼ δὲ ἀλλὰ ἡ χάρις τοῦ θεοῦ ἡ σὺν ἐμοί.
records.gloss: by grace but of God I am what I am, and the grace of him that toward me not empty became, but more than them all I labored, not I but but the grace of the God that [is] with me.
pieces: It is God's grace that has made me what I am, and {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} grace to me was not wasted. Instead, I have toiled harder than all of them, though it was not I but God's grace working with me.

L.10: But by [the] grace of God I am what I am, and {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} grace toward me did not turn out empty; rather, I toiled more than all of them, yet not I, but the grace of God that [is] with me.

R.10: But God in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} grace made me what I am, and that grace was not wasted on me. In fact, I have worked harder than all the other apostles. Yet it was not really I who did it. It was God's grace, which was with me.

decisions.choice: grace: God's undeserved favor, and the power at work in Paul
decisions.reason: χάριτι, χάρις and χάρις are the same word three times. Set against verse 9, it is favor Paul did nothing to earn. By the third time it is something active: the grace "with" him does the work.

decisions.choice: empty: without result
decisions.reason: κενὴ is the word Paul uses in verse 14 for preaching and faith that would be empty if Christ were not raised, and in verse 58 for work that is not in vain.

decisions.choice: more than all of them: either more than any one apostle or more than all of them together
decisions.reason: περισσότερον αὐτῶν πάντων can be read either way; the translation keeps both open.

decisions.choice: not I but grace: Paul does not deny his own effort, but gives the credit for it to God
decisions.reason: He has just said that he toiled. He then corrects himself, as in Galatians 2:20 and Philippians 2:12-13: the work was his, and yet it was God's grace working in him.

decisions.choice: God in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} grace made me what I am
alternatives: by the grace of God I am what I am
decisions.reason: Readable makes God the subject so that the sentence is easy to follow.

records.source: εἴτε οὖν ἐγὼ εἴτε ἐκεῖνοι, οὕτως κηρύσσομεν καὶ οὕτως ἐπιστεύσατε.
records.gloss: whether then I or those, so we proclaim and so you believed.
pieces: In any case, whether it came from me or from them, this is the message we all proclaim, and this is the message you believed.

L.11: Whether then [it was] I or they, so we proclaim and so you believed.

R.11: So it does not matter whether you heard it from me or from the other apostles. We all preach the same message, and it is this message that you believed.

decisions.choice: they: the other apostles and witnesses just named
decisions.reason: ἐκεῖνοι looks back to Cephas, the Twelve, James and the apostles in verses 5-7.

decisions.choice: so: this same message, the one set out in verses 3-5
decisions.reason: οὕτως and οὕτως point back to the gospel just summed up. All the apostles proclaim it, and the Corinthians believed it, which prepares the question of verse 12.

decisions.choice: this is the message we all proclaim
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "so" points to (m2).

records.source: Εἰ δὲ Χριστὸς κηρύσσεται ὅτι ἐκ νεκρῶν ἐγήγερται, πῶς λέγουσιν ἐν ὑμῖν τινες ὅτι ἀνάστασις νεκρῶν οὐκ ἔστιν;
records.gloss: If but Christ is proclaimed that from dead he has been raised, how say among you some that resurrection of dead not is?
pieces: Now if what we proclaim about {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} is that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has been raised from the dead, how can some among you be saying there is no such thing as a resurrection of the dead?

L.12: Now if {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} is proclaimed, that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has been raised from [the] dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of [the] dead?

R.12: We proclaim that God has raised {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} from the dead. So how can some of you say that the dead will never rise?

decisions.choice: if: a condition Paul takes as true, since Christ is in fact proclaimed
decisions.reason: Εἰ begins a chain of conditions that runs to verse 19. Here the "if" states what both sides accept; the following conditions draw out what the denial would mean.

decisions.choice: no resurrection of the dead: some at Corinth denied that dead people will be raised
decisions.reason: Paul does not say exactly what they believed. They may have held that the resurrection had already happened in a spiritual sense (compare 2 Timothy 2:18), or have found the idea of a raised body absurd, as verses 35-49 suggest. Either way they did not deny that Christ was raised, and Paul shows that the two stand or fall together.

decisions.choice: from the dead: from among dead people
decisions.reason: νεκρῶν is plural: Christ was raised out from among the dead. That is the link Paul uses: if one dead person has been raised, the dead can be raised.

decisions.choice: there is no such thing as a resurrection of the dead
alternatives: there is no resurrection of the dead
decisions.reason: Balanced gives the full force of the flat denial.

decisions.choice: God has raised
decisions.reason: Readable names God as the one who raised him, as Paul does in verse 15.

records.heading: If the dead are not raised

records.source: εἰ δὲ ἀνάστασις νεκρῶν οὐκ ἔστιν, οὐδὲ Χριστὸς ἐγήγερται·
records.gloss: if but resurrection of dead not is, neither Christ has been raised;
pieces: If there is no resurrection of the dead, then {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} has not been raised either.

L.13: But if there is no resurrection of [the] dead, not even {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} has been raised.

R.13: If the dead do not rise, then God has not raised {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} either.

decisions.choice: if there is none, then not even Christ: the general denial takes in Christ as well
decisions.reason: If no dead person can be raised, then Christ, who died, cannot have been. This is the first link in the chain that runs to verse 19. ἐγήγερται is again the perfect, "has been raised", as in verse 4.

decisions.choice: God has not raised
decisions.reason: As in verse 12, Readable names God as the one who raises.

records.source: εἰ δὲ Χριστὸς οὐκ ἐγήγερται, κενὸν ἄρα τὸ κήρυγμα ἡμῶν, κενὴ καὶ ἡ πίστις ὑμῶν, εὑρισκόμεθα δὲ καὶ ψευδομάρτυρες τοῦ θεοῦ, ὅτι ἐμαρτυρήσαμεν κατὰ τοῦ θεοῦ ὅτι ἤγειρεν τὸν Χριστόν, ὃν οὐκ ἤγειρεν εἴπερ ἄρα νεκροὶ οὐκ ἐγείρονται.
records.gloss: if but Christ not has been raised, empty then the proclamation of us, empty also the faith of you, \v 15 we are found but also false witnesses of the God, because we testified against the God that he raised the Christ, whom not he raised if indeed then dead not are raised.
pieces: And if {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} has not been raised, then what we proclaim is empty, and your faith is empty too.

Worse, we turn out to be giving false evidence about God, since we have borne witness against God by saying {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} raised {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, when {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} did not raise {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, if it is really so that the dead are not raised.

L.14: And if {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} has not been raised, then our proclamation [is] empty, and your faith [is] also empty,
L.15: and we are even found [to be] false witnesses of God, because we testified against God that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} raised the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, whom {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} did not raise if after all [the] dead are not raised.

R.14: And if {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} has not been raised, then our preaching is worth nothing, and so is your faith.
R.15: Even worse, we who preach would be telling lies about God. We have told everyone that God raised {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} from death. But if it is true that the dead do not rise, then God did not raise {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: empty: without content and without result
decisions.reason: κενὸν and κενὴ are the word used of grace in verse 10. Preaching about a Christ who was not raised would have nothing in it, and faith resting on it would have nothing to rest on.

decisions.choice: false witnesses of God: people who give false testimony about God
alternatives: false witnesses who claim to be sent by God
decisions.reason: The phrase is explained by what follows: they have testified that God did something he did not do.

decisions.choice: against God: to say falsely that God did something is to testify against him
decisions.reason: κατὰ with this case usually means "against". Paul uses the strong sense: a false claim about God's act would be testimony against God himself.

decisions.choice: he raised: God is the one who raised Christ
decisions.reason: ἤγειρεν makes plain who is behind the passive "has been raised" in verses 4, 12-14 and 20.

decisions.choice: we who preach ... told everyone
decisions.reason: Readable says who "we" are (the preachers of verse 11) and what their testimony was.

records.source: εἰ γὰρ νεκροὶ οὐκ ἐγείρονται, οὐδὲ Χριστὸς ἐγήγερται·
records.gloss: if for dead not are raised, neither Christ has been raised;
pieces: For if dead people are not raised, neither has {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} been raised.

L.16: For if [the] dead are not raised, not even {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} has been raised.

R.16: So if the dead do not rise, then God has not raised {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} either.

decisions.choice: for if the dead are not raised: Paul restates verse 13 to start the chain again
decisions.reason: ἐγείρονται is present tense, stating a general rule: the dead are never raised. Verses 16-18 repeat the logic of 13-15 and carry it further, to the believers' sins and to those who have died.

decisions.choice: God has not raised
decisions.reason: As in verses 12-13, Readable names God as the one who raises.

records.source: εἰ δὲ Χριστὸς οὐκ ἐγήγερται, ματαία ἡ πίστις ὑμῶν, ἔτι ἐστὲ ἐν ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ὑμῶν.
records.gloss: if but Christ not has been raised, futile the faith of you, still you are in the sins of you.
pieces: But if {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} has not been raised, your faith is worthless, and you are still in your sins.

L.17: But if {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} has not been raised, useless [is] your faith; still you are in your sins.

R.17: And if {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} has not been raised, your faith is useless. Your sins are still counted against you.

decisions.choice: futile: achieving nothing
decisions.reason: ματαία differs a little from "empty" in verse 14: there faith had nothing in it; here it gets nothing done. It cannot free them from their sins.

decisions.choice: still in your sins: unforgiven, still under sin's guilt
decisions.reason: Christ died "for our sins" (verse 3), and his being raised shows that his death has done its work (Romans 4:25). Without the resurrection, his death would have left their sins where they were.

decisions.choice: Your sins are still counted against you
alternatives: you are still in your sins
decisions.reason: Readable says what being "in" one's sins means (m2).

records.source: ἄρα καὶ οἱ κοιμηθέντες ἐν Χριστῷ ἀπώλοντο.
records.gloss: then also those having fallen asleep in Christ perished.
pieces: It would also mean that those who have died in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} have perished.

L.18: Then also those who fell asleep in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} perished.

R.18: It would also mean that people who died trusting in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} are lost forever.

decisions.choice: fallen asleep: died
decisions.reason: As in verse 6, 7:39 and 11:30. The image of sleep implies waking; if there is no resurrection, the image is empty.

decisions.choice: in Christ: belonging to Christ, united with him when they died
decisions.reason: ἐν Χριστῷ describes believers who died, as "the dead in Christ" does in 1 Thessalonians 4:16.

decisions.choice: perished: lost and ruined beyond hope, not simply dead
decisions.reason: ἀπώλοντο is the verb used in 1:18 of "those who are perishing". If Christ was not raised, those who trusted him have no future at all.

decisions.choice: have died; died
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the meaning of the idiom (m1), as in verse 6; Literal keeps it.

decisions.choice: trusting in; lost forever
decisions.reason: Readable says what "in Christ" and "perished" mean here (m2, m3).

records.source: εἰ ἐν τῇ ζωῇ ταύτῃ ἐν Χριστῷ ἠλπικότες ἐσμὲν μόνον, ἐλεεινότεροι πάντων ἀνθρώπων ἐσμέν.
records.gloss: if in the life this in Christ having hoped we are only, more pitiable than all people we are.
pieces: If our hope in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} reaches no further than this life, no one is more to be pitied than we are.

L.19: If in this life we have hoped in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, and only [that], we are more pitiable than all {{gender:people|men}}.

R.19: If our hope in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} is only for this life, then people should feel sorrier for us than for anyone else.

decisions.choice: only: a hope that goes no further than this life
alternatives: if hoping is all we have done, with nothing to hope for
decisions.reason: μόνον stands at the end of the clause and could limit the whole of it. Read with ἐν τῇ ζωῇ ταύτῃ ("in this life"), it means a hope that ends at death, which fits verses 18 and 32.

decisions.choice: we have hoped: a settled hope placed in Christ
decisions.reason: ἠλπικότες ἐσμὲν is a perfect: they have set their hope on Christ and it stays there.

decisions.choice: more pitiable: more to be pitied, because they have given up so much for a hope that would be false
decisions.reason: Verses 30-32 show what Paul has given up and risked. If the hope ends at death, all of that was for nothing.

decisions.choice: no one is more to be pitied than we are
alternatives: we are more pitiable than all people
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the comparison in natural English order.

records.source: Νυνὶ δὲ Χριστὸς ἐγήγερται ἐκ νεκρῶν, ἀπαρχὴ τῶν κεκοιμημένων.
records.gloss: Now but Christ has been raised from dead, firstfruits of those having fallen asleep.
pieces: But as it is, {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} has been raised from the dead: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is the firstfruits of those who have died.

L.20: But now {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} has been raised from [the] dead, [the] firstfruits of those who sleep.

R.20: But {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} truly has been raised from the dead. He is the firstfruits, like the first part of a harvest, and those who have died will follow {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} as the rest of the harvest.

decisions.choice: but now: as things really are
decisions.reason: Νυνὶ δὲ marks the turn from the false supposition of verses 13-19 to the fact. Paul again uses the perfect, "has been raised".

decisions.choice: firstfruits: the first part of the harvest, given to God, which promised the rest
decisions.reason: Israel brought the first sheaf of the barley harvest to the priest to be offered to God before the rest was gathered (Leviticus 23:9-14). The first part belongs to the whole harvest and shows that the rest will come. Christ's being raised is the start of the resurrection of all who belong to him (verse 23). The sheaf was offered in the days after Passover, the time of Jesus' death and resurrection, but Paul does not draw out that link.

decisions.choice: those who have fallen asleep: believers who have died
decisions.reason: As in verses 6 and 18. κεκοιμημένων is a perfect: they have died and remain in death, waiting to be raised.

decisions.choice: those who have died
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the meaning of the idiom (m3), as in verses 6 and 18; Literal keeps it.

decisions.choice: like the first part of a harvest ... will follow {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} as the rest of the harvest
alternatives: the firstfruits of those who have died
decisions.reason: Readable explains the picture (m2).

records.heading: The firstfruits of those who have died

records.source: ἐπειδὴ γὰρ δι’ ἀνθρώπου θάνατος, καὶ δι’ ἀνθρώπου ἀνάστασις νεκρῶν·
records.gloss: since for through a human being death, also through a human being resurrection of dead;
pieces: For since death came by way of a human being, the resurrection of the dead also comes by way of a human being.

L.21: For since through a human being [came] death, also through a human being [comes the] resurrection of [the] dead.

R.21: Death came through one human being, Adam. And rising from the dead comes through another human being, {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.

decisions.choice: a human being: Adam in the first case, Christ in the second, each a human being
decisions.reason: ἀνθρώπου and ἀνθρώπου mean a human being. The point is that both death and resurrection came through someone human; for Christ, it stresses that he shares our humanity. Each refers to one particular person, so no inclusive setting applies.

decisions.choice: came ... comes: the verbs are left out in the Greek
decisions.reason: The sentence has no verbs. Death came through Adam in the past; resurrection comes through Christ, begun in him and still to come for others (verses 22-23).

decisions.choice: the two human beings: Adam brought death, Christ brings life
decisions.reason: Paul makes the same comparison at length in Romans 5:12-21, and again in verses 45-49 of this chapter.

decisions.choice: a human being
decisions.reason: "A human being" keeps the stress on humanity (m1). Readable says the same.

decisions.choice: Adam; {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}
decisions.reason: Readable names the two people, as verse 22 does.

records.source: ὥσπερ γὰρ ἐν τῷ Ἀδὰμ πάντες ἀποθνῄσκουσιν, οὕτως καὶ ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ πάντες ζῳοποιηθήσονται.
records.gloss: as for in the Adam all die, so also in the Christ all will be made alive.
pieces: Just as all who belong to Adam die, so all who belong to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} will be brought to life.

L.22: For just as in Adam all die, so also in the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} all will be made alive.

R.22: All people die because they are joined to Adam. In the same way, all who are joined to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} will be brought to life.

decisions.choice: in Adam ... in Christ: all who are united with Adam die; all who are united with Christ will be made alive
alternatives: all people without exception will be made alive
decisions.reason: "In" names belonging to a head. Everyone belongs to Adam; verse 23 says that those made alive are "those who belong to Christ", at his coming. So the second "all" is everyone in Christ.

decisions.choice: will be made alive: raised to life at the resurrection
decisions.reason: ζῳοποιηθήσονται is future and looks to the resurrection at Christ's coming (verse 23), not the new life believers have now.

decisions.choice: all who belong to; joined to
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "in" means here (m1).

records.source: ἕκαστος δὲ ἐν τῷ ἰδίῳ τάγματι· ἀπαρχὴ Χριστός, ἔπειτα οἱ τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐν τῇ παρουσίᾳ αὐτοῦ·
records.gloss: each but in the own order; firstfruits Christ, then those of the Christ at the coming of him;
pieces: But each has a set place in the sequence: first {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, the firstfruits; after that, at {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} coming, the people who are {{deity_pronoun:his|His}}.

L.23: But each one in [their] own order: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} [the] firstfruits, then those who are the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}'s at {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} coming.

R.23: But it happens in the right order. {{christos:Christ|The Messiah}} was raised first, as the firstfruits. Then, when {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} comes back, the people who belong to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} will be raised.

decisions.choice: order: a place in a sequence
decisions.reason: τάγματι was used of a rank or unit of soldiers. Here the point is sequence: Christ first, then those who are his.

decisions.choice: coming: Christ's arrival at the end
decisions.reason: παρουσίᾳ means presence or arrival. Paul uses it of the arrival of friends (16:17; 2 Corinthians 7:6), and of the Lord's coming (1 Thessalonians 2:19; 4:15). The word was also used for the visit of a ruler.

decisions.choice: those of Christ: the people who belong to Christ
decisions.reason: Paul speaks here only of believers being raised; he does not discuss others in this chapter.

decisions.choice: was raised first; will be raised
decisions.reason: Readable supplies the verb the Greek leaves out.

records.source: εἶτα τὸ τέλος, ὅταν παραδιδῷ τὴν βασιλείαν τῷ θεῷ καὶ πατρί, ὅταν καταργήσῃ πᾶσαν ἀρχὴν καὶ πᾶσαν ἐξουσίαν καὶ δύναμιν, δεῖ γὰρ αὐτὸν βασιλεύειν ἄχρι οὗ θῇ πάντας τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ὑπὸ τοὺς πόδας αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: then the end, when he hands over the kingdom to the God and Father, when he does away with all rule and all authority and power. \v 25 It is necessary for him to reign until which he puts all the enemies under the feet of him.
pieces: After that comes the end, when {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} hands the kingdom over to God the Father, once {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has put an end to every ruler, every authority and every power.
For {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} reign must continue until {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has placed all {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} enemies beneath {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} feet.

L.24: Then [comes] the end, when {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} hands over the kingdom to God, even [the] Father, when {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has done away with every rule and every authority and power.
L.25: For {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} must reign until {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has put all the enemies under {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} feet.

R.24: Then the end will come. {{christos:Christ|The Messiah}} will give the kingdom to God the Father, once {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has put an end to every ruler, every authority and every power that opposes God.
R.25: For {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} must rule as king until all {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} enemies have been put under {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} feet.

decisions.choice: he hands over, he does away with, he must reign: Christ
decisions.reason: Christ is the subject from verse 23, and he hands the kingdom to God the Father.

decisions.choice: until he has put: most naturally Christ, continuing the subject; under his feet: Christ's
alternatives: God puts the enemies under Christ's feet, as in Psalm 110:1, where God speaks to the king
decisions.reason: The subject of θῇ is not stated. The run of the sentence points to Christ; the Psalm and verse 27, where God subjects all things to Christ, point to God. Either way the enemies end up under Christ's feet.

decisions.choice: Psalm 110:1
decisions.reason: In Psalm 110:1 the LORD (the divine name in the Hebrew) says to the king, "Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet." Paul alludes to it in his own words, and joins the phrase "under his feet" from Psalm 8:7, which he quotes in verse 27.

decisions.choice: rule, authority, power: the powers, seen and unseen, that oppose God
decisions.reason: The same words name hostile powers in 2:6-8, Ephesians 1:21 and Colossians 2:15. Here they are among the "enemies" of verse 25.

decisions.choice: hands over the kingdom: when every enemy is defeated, the Son gives the kingdom to the Father, and his work of subduing reaches its goal
decisions.reason: Paul describes the end of Christ's work of conquering, not a loss of his honor. Verse 28 says more about the Son's place; Philippians 2:9-11 likewise ends Christ's exaltation in the glory of God the Father.

decisions.choice: the end: the close of the present age
alternatives: the rest, the remaining people to be raised
decisions.reason: τέλος can mean "the rest", which would continue the list of verse 23, but its usual sense in Paul is the end (1:8; 10:11), and what follows describes the end of all things.

decisions.choice: put an end to
decisions.reason: The verb means to make powerless or do away with; Literal says "done away with", as in 2 Corinthians 3.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|The Messiah}}; that opposes God; have been put under {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} feet
decisions.reason: Readable names Christ, says that these powers are hostile (m4), and uses a passive so as not to decide who puts the enemies under his feet (m2).

records.source: ἔσχατος ἐχθρὸς καταργεῖται ὁ θάνατος, πάντα γὰρ ὑπέταξεν ὑπὸ τοὺς πόδας αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: last enemy is being done away with, the death; \v 27 all things for he subjected under the feet of him.
pieces: The last enemy to be done away with is death.
For "{{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has placed everything in subjection beneath {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} feet."

L.26: [The] last enemy is being done away with: death.
L.27: For "{{deity_pronoun:he|He}} subjected all things under {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} feet."

R.26: The last enemy that will be destroyed is death.
R.27: For Scripture says that God has put everything under the feet of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.

decisions.choice: is being done away with: certain to happen, and already set in motion by Christ's resurrection
alternatives: simply future, will be done away with
decisions.reason: καταργεῖται is present tense. It can state a certain future as if already happening; the work has begun, since Christ has been raised.

decisions.choice: death, the last enemy: death is spoken of as a hostile power, the last to be defeated
decisions.reason: Death came through Adam (verse 21) and rules over all people (Romans 5:14, 17). Its defeat is the resurrection itself (verses 54-55).

decisions.choice: Psalm 8:7
decisions.reason: The Psalm says of humankind that God has "put all things under his feet". Paul applies it to Christ, the human being through whom the rule given to humankind is fulfilled (verse 21; compare Ephesians 1:22; Hebrews 2:6-9). He changes "you" to "he".

decisions.choice: he subjected: God, the one addressed in the Psalm; under his feet: Christ's
alternatives: Christ put all things under his own feet
decisions.reason: In the Psalm, God is the one who subjects all things. Verses 27-28 confirm it: God is "the one who subjected all things to him".

decisions.choice: Scripture says that God has put everything under the feet of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}
alternatives: For "{{deity_pronoun:he|He}} subjected all things under {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} feet"
decisions.reason: Readable says that this is a quotation and names God and Christ (m3, m4).

records.source: ὅταν δὲ εἴπῃ ὅτι πάντα ὑποτέτακται, δῆλον ὅτι ἐκτὸς τοῦ ὑποτάξαντος αὐτῷ τὰ πάντα.
records.gloss: when but it says that all things have been subjected, clear that except the [one] having subjected to him the all things.
pieces: Now when Scripture says that all things have been placed in subjection, it is obvious that this does not include the one who placed all things in subjection to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

L.27: But when [it] says, "All things have been subjected," [it is] clear that [this is] apart from the one who subjected all things to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.27: Scripture says that everything has been put under {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}. But clearly this does not include God {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}, who put everything under {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: when it says: when Scripture, God speaking in the Psalm just quoted, says
alternatives: when Christ declares at the end that all things are subjected to him
decisions.reason: The subject of εἴπῃ is not stated. It most naturally refers back to the quotation in verse 27a. Some read ὅταν as "when" in the future, when Christ announces his completed victory.

decisions.choice: apart from the one who subjected: God, who subjects all things to Christ, is not himself among the things subjected
decisions.reason: "The one who subjected" is God and "to him" is Christ. Paul guards against reading "all things" so widely that it includes God.

decisions.choice: Scripture says
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say who speaks (m1); Literal keeps the bare verb.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}; God {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}
decisions.reason: Readable names the two persons (m2).

records.source: ὅταν δὲ ὑποταγῇ αὐτῷ τὰ πάντα, τότε αὐτὸς ὁ υἱὸς ὑποταγήσεται τῷ ὑποτάξαντι αὐτῷ τὰ πάντα, ἵνα ᾖ ὁ θεὸς πάντα ἐν πᾶσιν.
records.gloss: when but are subjected to him the all things, then himself the son will be subjected to the [one] having subjected to him the all things, so that may be the God all in all.
pieces: And once all things have been made subject to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, the Son {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}} will then be made subject to the one who made all things subject to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, so that God may be all in all.

L.28: And when all things have been subjected to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, then the Son {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}} will be subjected to the one who subjected all things to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, so that God may be all in all.

R.28: When everything has been put under the Son, then the Son {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}} will put {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}} under God, who put everything under {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. Then God will be all in all, ruling over everything completely.

decisions.choice: to him: Christ; the one who subjected: God
decisions.reason: As in verse 27, "the one who subjected" is God, and the one to whom all things are subjected is Christ, here called "the Son".

decisions.choice: the Son himself will be subjected: when his work is complete, the Son places himself and his kingdom under the Father
decisions.reason: Paul speaks of the Son's place in God's work of saving and ruling, in which the Son does the Father's will (compare 3:23; 11:3; Philippians 2:8-11). He does not say that the Son is a lesser being or that he stops reigning. How this fits with the Son's oneness with the Father has been discussed in the church since early times; the text states the order and does not explain it further.

decisions.choice: will be subjected: the Son's own willing act
alternatives: the Son will be made subject by God
decisions.reason: ὑποταγήσεται is passive in form, matching the other forms of the verb in these verses, and such forms are often used for an act a person does to himself. Nothing in the passage suggests that the Son is made subject against his will.

decisions.choice: all in all: God's rule is complete and unopposed in everything
alternatives: God becomes everything, so that all things are merged into God
decisions.reason: The whole passage is about enemies being defeated and all things being subjected. The phrase describes God's full and unchallenged rule, not the merging of creation into God.

decisions.choice: follow the SBLGNT: "then the Son himself"
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts add "also" before "the Son himself"; others, including some early ones, lack it. The sense hardly changes. Reviewers must check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: will put {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}} under God
decisions.reason: Readable expresses the Son's willing act (m3).

decisions.choice: ruling over everything completely
decisions.reason: Readable explains "all in all" (m4).

records.source: Ἐπεὶ τί ποιήσουσιν οἱ βαπτιζόμενοι ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν;
records.gloss: Otherwise what will they do those being baptized for the dead?
pieces: Otherwise, what will those who are baptized on behalf of the dead accomplish?

L.29: Otherwise, what will they do, those being baptized on behalf of the dead?

R.29: Think about the people who are baptized for the dead. If there is no resurrection, what will they gain by it?

decisions.choice: baptized for the dead: a practice the Corinthians knew; what it was is not known
alternatives: living believers were baptized in place of believers who had died unbaptized
people were baptized for the sake of believing relatives or friends who had died, so as to be united with them at the resurrection
"the dead" are the baptized themselves, whose bodies are dying, or who are baptized with a view to the dead being raised
decisions.reason: Nothing else in the New Testament or in other early writings explains this practice, and many proposals have been made. Paul neither approves nor condemns it. He speaks of "they", not "you" or "we", and uses it only to show that it makes no sense if the dead are not raised. The translation keeps the phrase as open as the Greek.

decisions.choice: for: on behalf of, for the sake of
decisions.reason: ὑπὲρ usually means "on behalf of" or "for the sake of". The other senses have been suggested in order to make the practice easier to explain.

decisions.choice: otherwise: that is, if the dead are not raised
decisions.reason: Ἐπεὶ takes up the argument of verses 12-19 again after verses 20-28.

decisions.choice: If there is no resurrection
decisions.reason: Readable says what "otherwise" stands for (m3).

records.source: εἰ ὅλως νεκροὶ οὐκ ἐγείρονται, τί καὶ βαπτίζονται ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν;
records.gloss: if at all dead not are raised, why also are they baptized for them?
pieces: If the dead are not raised at all, what is the point of being baptized for them?

L.29: If [the] dead are not raised at all, why indeed are they baptized on behalf of them?

R.29: If dead people never rise, why would anyone be baptized for them?

decisions.choice: at all: no dead person is ever raised
decisions.reason: ὅλως sharpens the denial Paul is answering (verse 12).

decisions.choice: they ... them: Paul speaks of the practice from outside, without saying he approves of it
decisions.reason: See the note on the previous sentence.

decisions.choice: what is the point
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the force of the question: the practice would be pointless.

records.source: τί καὶ ἡμεῖς κινδυνεύομεν πᾶσαν ὥραν;
records.gloss: why also we are in danger every hour?
pieces: And why do we ourselves put our lives at risk hour after hour?

L.30: Why also do we face danger every hour?

R.30: And why would I and those who work with me put our lives in danger all the time?

decisions.choice: we: Paul and those who preach with him
decisions.reason: ἡμεῖς is emphatic and set against "they" in verse 29. Verses 31-32 go on to Paul's own dangers.

decisions.choice: every hour: all the time
decisions.reason: πᾶσαν ὥραν; means constantly, not hour by hour.

decisions.choice: I and those who work with me
decisions.reason: Readable says who "we" are (m1).

records.source: καθ’ ἡμέραν ἀποθνῄσκω, νὴ τὴν ὑμετέραν καύχησιν, ἣν ἔχω ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ τῷ κυρίῳ ἡμῶν.
records.gloss: Daily I die, by the your boasting, which I have in Christ Jesus the Lord of us.
pieces: I die every day. I swear it by how proud I am of you in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus our Lord.

L.31: Every day I die; [I swear it] by the boasting about you that I have in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus our Lord.

R.31: Every day I am facing death. I promise you this is true, as surely as I am proud of you. And that pride is something I have through {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus our Lord.

decisions.choice: I die every day: I face death, my life is constantly at risk
alternatives: I die to myself every day
decisions.reason: The context is danger (verses 30, 32). Paul speaks the same way in 2 Corinthians 4:10-11 and 11:23 ("often near death"). The sense is not spiritual self-denial.

decisions.choice: by my boasting about you: an oath, sworn by Paul's pride in the Corinthians
decisions.reason: νὴ introduces an oath. ὑμετέραν ("your") names the object of the boasting, as Paul's pride in his converts (2 Corinthians 7:4; Philippians 2:16). It is a pride he has "in Christ Jesus", because the Lord did the work (verse 10).

decisions.choice: follow the SBLGNT, without "brothers"
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts, some of them early, add "brothers" after "your boasting"; others lack it. Reviewers must check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: how proud I am of you (B); I am proud of you (R)
decisions.reason: The book's boasting rule: Literal keeps "boasting"; Balanced and Readable say "proud", since the argument does not turn on the word here.

decisions.choice: I am facing death
decisions.reason: Readable says what the idiom means (m1).

records.source: εἰ κατὰ ἄνθρωπον ἐθηριομάχησα ἐν Ἐφέσῳ, τί μοι τὸ ὄφελος;
records.gloss: if according to human I fought wild beasts in Ephesus, what to me the gain?
pieces: If my fight with wild beasts in Ephesus was only for this life's sake, what good has it done me?

L.32: If in human terms I fought wild beasts in Ephesus, what [is] the gain to me?

R.32: In Ephesus I fought with wild beasts. If I did that only for what this life can give, what good was it to me?

decisions.choice: fought wild beasts: most likely a picture of fierce human opponents
alternatives: a real fight with animals in the arena
decisions.reason: Paul faced violent opposition in Ephesus (16:9; Acts 19:23-41) and deadly danger in Asia (2 Corinthians 1:8-10). A Roman citizen was not normally sent to the beasts, few survived it, and neither Acts nor Paul's list of sufferings in 2 Corinthians 11:23-27 mentions it. Still, it cannot be ruled out. The translation keeps the picture at every level.

decisions.choice: in human terms: with merely human hopes, for what this life can give
alternatives: humanly speaking, a sign that the words are a figure of speech
decisions.reason: κατὰ ἄνθρωπον can mean either. The sentences around it are about hope limited to this life (verses 19 and 32b), so the first sense fits best.

decisions.choice: only for this life's sake (B); only for what this life can give (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable spell out the sense chosen (m2).

records.source: εἰ νεκροὶ οὐκ ἐγείρονται, Φάγωμεν καὶ πίωμεν, αὔριον γὰρ ἀποθνῄσκομεν.
records.gloss: if dead not are raised, Let us eat and let us drink, tomorrow for we die.
pieces: If the dead are not raised, then "Let us eat and drink, since tomorrow we die."

L.32: If [the] dead are not raised, "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die."

R.32: If the dead do not rise, we might as well say, "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die."

decisions.choice: Isaiah 22:13
decisions.reason: The words match the Greek Old Testament of Isaiah 22:13 exactly. There the people of Jerusalem feast when they should be mourning and turning back to God. Paul uses the words for the outlook of people who expect nothing after death.

decisions.choice: we die: a present tense for what is about to happen
decisions.reason: ἀποθνῄσκομεν is present in form; death is near and certain.

decisions.choice: we might as well say
decisions.reason: Readable shows that this is the conclusion someone without hope would draw.

records.source: μὴ πλανᾶσθε· φθείρουσιν ἤθη χρηστὰ ὁμιλίαι κακαί.
records.gloss: not be deceived; ruin morals good companies bad.
pieces: Make no mistake: "Good character is ruined by bad company."

L.33: Do not be led astray: "Bad associations ruin good morals."

R.33: Do not fool yourselves. As the saying goes, "If you spend time with bad people, they will spoil your good ways."

decisions.choice: a well-known Greek saying, a line from the poet Menander
decisions.reason: The line comes from the comedy Thais by the Athenian poet Menander (fourth to third century BC) and had become a common saying. Paul quotes it as a proverb; it does not show that he had read Menander.

decisions.choice: company: the people one spends time and talks with
decisions.reason: ὁμιλίαι can mean both. In context the bad company is those who say there is no resurrection (verses 12, 34), whose outlook leads to the life of verse 32.

decisions.choice: do not be led astray: stop letting yourselves be deceived
decisions.reason: μὴ πλανᾶσθε is a present command, as in 6:9: they are already in danger of being misled.

decisions.choice: Make no mistake
decisions.reason: As in 6:9.

decisions.choice: As the saying goes
decisions.reason: Readable shows that this is a well-known saying (m1).

records.source: ἐκνήψατε δικαίως καὶ μὴ ἁμαρτάνετε, ἀγνωσίαν γὰρ θεοῦ τινες ἔχουσιν· πρὸς ἐντροπὴν ὑμῖν λαλῶ.
records.gloss: Sober up rightly and not sin, ignorance for of God some have; toward shame to you I speak.
pieces: Sober up, as you should, and stop sinning. There are some who do not know God at all. I say this to shame you.

L.34: Sober up properly and stop sinning, for some have ignorance of God; I speak to your shame.

R.34: Come to your senses, as you should, and stop sinning. Some of you do not really know God. I am saying this to make you ashamed.

decisions.choice: sober up: wake up from a drunken stupor, come back to one's senses
decisions.reason: ἐκνήψατε was used of becoming sober after drinking. It answers the slogan of verse 32, "let us eat and drink".

decisions.choice: properly: as is right
decisions.reason: δικαίως is an adverb meaning rightly or as one should. It describes how they are to sober up, not a goal.

decisions.choice: stop sinning: a present command, to stop what they are doing
decisions.reason: μὴ ἁμαρτάνετε is a present command; in context it means to stop going on in sin.

decisions.choice: ignorance of God: they do not know God himself, or his power to raise the dead
decisions.reason: Jesus says the same of those who denied the resurrection (Matthew 22:29). It is sharp, since the Corinthians prided themselves on knowledge (8:1). "Some" are the people of verse 12.

decisions.choice: Come to your senses
decisions.reason: Readable gives the meaning of the picture; Literal and Balanced keep it.

decisions.choice: I say this to shame you
decisions.reason: As in 6:5.

records.source: Ἀλλὰ ἐρεῖ τις· Πῶς ἐγείρονται οἱ νεκροί, ποίῳ δὲ σώματι ἔρχονται;
records.gloss: But will say someone: How are raised the dead, with what kind and body do they come?
pieces: But someone will object, "How are dead people raised? And what sort of body will they have when they come back?"

L.35: But someone will say, "How are the dead raised, and with what sort of body do they come?"

R.35: But someone may ask, "How are dead people raised to life? What kind of body will they have?"

decisions.choice: someone will say: an imagined questioner whose objection Paul answers
decisions.reason: Paul uses a common way of arguing in his day: he puts a question in the mouth of an imagined opponent and then answers it (as in Romans 9:19). The question takes up the doubt of those in Corinth who said there is no resurrection of the dead (verse 12).

decisions.choice: two questions: how can the dead be raised at all, and what kind of body will they have
decisions.reason: The first question doubts that resurrection is possible; the second asks what body the dead could have once their bodies have decayed. Paul answers the second at length (verses 36-49), and in doing so answers the first. The present tenses ἐγείρονται ("are raised") and ἔρχονται ("do they come") speak of resurrection in general, not of something already happening.

decisions.choice: object (B); ask (R); will they have when they come back (B); will they have (R)
alternatives: with what body do they come
decisions.reason: The words introduce a question, so Balanced says "object" (m2) and Readable "ask". "Come" means to come back from death at the resurrection; Readable leaves it out because the question is plain without it.

records.heading: The resurrection body

records.source: ἄφρων, σὺ ὃ σπείρεις, οὐ ζῳοποιεῖται ἐὰν μὴ ἀποθάνῃ·
records.gloss: Fool! you, what you sow not is made alive unless it dies;
pieces: How foolish! A seed you sow does not come alive unless it dies.

L.36: Fool! What you yourself sow is not made alive unless it dies.

R.36: How foolish you are! When you plant a seed, it does not come alive unless it first dies.

decisions.choice: fool: someone who is not thinking, who misses what is plain
decisions.reason: ἄφρων means without sense or understanding (Luke 12:20; 2 Corinthians 11:16-19). It is a sharp rebuke, of the kind used in the style of argument begun in verse 35, aimed at the imagined questioner, not at the Corinthians as a whole.

decisions.choice: you yourself: the questioner's own farming already answers the question
decisions.reason: The pronoun σὺ is not needed with the verb and so is emphatic: the one who asks how the dead can live sows seed and sees it every year.

decisions.choice: made alive: brought to new life, the verb Paul uses of the resurrection
decisions.reason: ζῳοποιεῖται is the verb of verse 22 ("in Christ all will be made alive") and verse 45 ("a life-giving spirit"). The seed is a picture of the body: life comes through death, as Jesus also said of a grain of wheat (John 12:24).

decisions.choice: Fool! (L); How foolish! (B); How foolish you are! (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable keep the rebuke but make it an exclamation, which sounds natural in English.

decisions.choice: A seed you sow (B); When you plant a seed, first (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the seed, which verse 37 makes explicit. Readable says "plant" for "sow" and adds "first" to show the order.

records.source: καὶ ὃ σπείρεις, οὐ τὸ σῶμα τὸ γενησόμενον σπείρεις ἀλλὰ γυμνὸν κόκκον εἰ τύχοι σίτου ἤ τινος τῶν λοιπῶν·
records.gloss: And what you sow, not the body that will be you sow but a bare grain, if it may happen, of wheat or of some of the rest;
pieces: When you sow, you are not sowing the body that will grow, but a bare seed, perhaps of wheat or of some other grain.

L.37: And what you sow, you do not sow the body that will be, but a bare grain, perhaps of wheat or of some of the rest.

R.37: And what you plant is not the full-grown plant. It is only a bare seed, maybe wheat or some other kind of grain.

decisions.choice: a bare grain: a seed without the stalk, leaves and ear it will have
alternatives: a seed with its husk removed
decisions.reason: γυμνὸν means naked or bare. The seed in the ground has none of the form of the plant that grows from it. The word prepares for the clothing language of verses 53-54, where the body "puts on" imperishability (compare 2 Corinthians 5:3).

decisions.choice: the body that will be: the plant that comes from the seed, the same life in a new form
alternatives: a different thing that replaces the seed
decisions.reason: Paul's picture holds two things together: what grows comes from what was sown, and yet it looks very different. So the resurrection body is joined to the present one, and yet is changed (verses 42-44).

decisions.choice: perhaps: for example
alternatives: "if it should happen" as a real condition
decisions.reason: εἰ τύχοι ("if it may happen") is a fixed phrase meaning "perhaps" or "for example", as in 14:10.

decisions.choice: the full-grown plant
decisions.reason: Readable says what "the body that will be" means in the picture of the seed (m2).

records.source: ὁ δὲ θεὸς δίδωσιν αὐτῷ σῶμα καθὼς ἠθέλησεν, καὶ ἑκάστῳ τῶν σπερμάτων ἴδιον σῶμα.
records.gloss: The but God gives to it a body as he willed, and to each of the seeds its own body.
pieces: God gives it the body {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has chosen, and gives each kind of seed a body of its own.

L.38: But God gives it a body as {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} willed, and to each of the seeds its own body.

R.38: Then God gives it the body {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has chosen for it. Each kind of seed gets its own kind of body.

decisions.choice: God gives the body: the new form is God's gift, not something the seed makes for itself
alternatives: the seed grows into its body by nature alone
decisions.reason: The subject is God, set against "you" who sow (verses 36-37). The present δίδωσιν ("gives") speaks of God's work in every harvest. The same God gives the dead their new body.

decisions.choice: as he willed: by God's decision at creation, each kind with its own body
decisions.reason: The past tense ἠθέλησεν ("he willed") looks back to God's decision, most likely at creation, when plants were made to bear seed "each according to its kind" (Genesis 1:11-12). The list of creatures in verse 39 follows the same account.

decisions.choice: each kind of seed
decisions.reason: Paul means the different kinds of seed, each with its own plant; Balanced and Readable add "kind".

records.source: οὐ πᾶσα σὰρξ ἡ αὐτὴ σάρξ, ἀλλὰ ἄλλη μὲν ἀνθρώπων, ἄλλη δὲ σὰρξ κτηνῶν, ἄλλη δὲ σὰρξ πτηνῶν, ἄλλη δὲ ἰχθύων.
records.gloss: Not all flesh [is] the same flesh, but one indeed of humans, another and flesh of beasts, another and flesh of birds, another and of fish.
pieces: Flesh is not all of one kind. Human flesh is one thing, the flesh of animals another, the flesh of birds another, and that of fish another.

L.39: Not all flesh [is] the same flesh, but one [is] of human beings, another flesh of beasts, another flesh of birds, another of fish.

R.39: Living things do not all have the same kind of flesh. People have one kind, animals have another, and birds and fish have others.

decisions.choice: flesh: the physical stuff of living bodies
decisions.reason: σὰρξ has many senses in Paul. Elsewhere in these letters it often means what is merely human (1:26; 3:3), but here it means the bodily flesh of people, animals, birds and fish. Paul's point is that God has made many different kinds of bodies.

decisions.choice: humans, beasts, birds, fish: the living creatures of the creation account
alternatives: a list with no particular source
decisions.reason: The four kinds recall the creatures of Genesis 1:20-26, named in the reverse order. κτηνῶν means animals, especially domestic animals and cattle.

decisions.choice: flesh
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice for this word at Balanced and Readable is "by human standards", but that sense does not fit here (m1), so every level says "flesh".

decisions.choice: beasts (L); animals (B, R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the older word; Balanced and Readable use the everyday one.

records.source: καὶ σώματα ἐπουράνια, καὶ σώματα ἐπίγεια· ἀλλὰ ἑτέρα μὲν ἡ τῶν ἐπουρανίων δόξα, ἑτέρα δὲ ἡ τῶν ἐπιγείων.
records.gloss: And bodies heavenly, and bodies earthly; but different indeed the of the heavenly glory, different and that of the earthly.
pieces: Some bodies belong to the heavens and some to the earth, and the glory of those in the heavens differs from the glory of those on earth.

L.40: And [there are] heavenly bodies and earthly bodies; but the glory of the heavenly [is] one thing, and that of the earthly [is] another.

R.40: There are bodies in the sky and bodies on the earth. The bodies in the sky have one kind of glory, and the bodies on the earth have another kind.

decisions.choice: heavenly bodies: the sun, moon and stars
alternatives: the bodies of the raised dead
decisions.reason: Verse 41 names the sun, moon and stars, so ἐπουράνια here means the bodies that are seen in the sky. Some have taken it as angels, but the next verse makes the meaning plain.

decisions.choice: glory: visible splendor, brightness and beauty
decisions.reason: δόξα can mean honor, but here it is the splendor that can be seen, the shining of the sun and the stars (verse 41). Paul uses the same word for the raised body in verse 43.

decisions.choice: belong to the heavens (B); in the sky (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the wording of heaven and earth; Readable says where the sun, moon and stars are seen.

records.source: ἄλλη δόξα ἡλίου, καὶ ἄλλη δόξα σελήνης, καὶ ἄλλη δόξα ἀστέρων, ἀστὴρ γὰρ ἀστέρος διαφέρει ἐν δόξῃ.
records.gloss: Another glory of sun, and another glory of moon, and another glory of stars, star for from star differs in glory.
pieces: The sun has its own glory, the moon another, the stars another; and even among the stars, each has a glory that is different.

L.41: One [is the] glory of [the] sun, and another [the] glory of [the] moon, and another [the] glory of [the] stars; for star differs from star in glory.

R.41: The sun shines with one kind of glory, the moon with another, and the stars with another. And each star shines with a glory different from the others.

decisions.choice: for star differs from star: even within one kind God has made variety
alternatives: a reason for the sentence before
decisions.reason: γὰρ ("for") adds a further example rather than a strict reason: not only do sun, moon and stars differ, but one star differs from another.

decisions.choice: the point is the variety of bodies God has made, preparing for the contrast in verses 42-44
alternatives: different levels of reward or glory for believers in heaven
decisions.reason: Paul is answering the question of verse 35, what kind of body the dead will have. The examples show that God can give a body of a quite different glory from the present one. The verse is not about ranks among the raised.

decisions.choice: shines with (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says what the glory of the sun and stars is, their brightness (40 m2).

records.source: Οὕτως καὶ ἡ ἀνάστασις τῶν νεκρῶν.
records.gloss: So also the resurrection of the dead.
pieces: It is the same with the resurrection of the dead.

L.42: So also [is] the resurrection of the dead.

R.42: This is how it will be when the dead are raised.

decisions.choice: so also: the seed and the different glories show what the resurrection is like
alternatives: only the last example, the stars
decisions.reason: Οὕτως ("so") draws the pictures of verses 36-41 together: as the plant differs from the seed and one body from another, the raised body differs from the body that died.

decisions.choice: resurrection: the dead raised to bodily life
decisions.reason: ἀνάστασις is the word of verses 12-13 and 21. It means rising up, and Paul speaks of it as something that happens to the body (verses 35, 44).

decisions.choice: when the dead are raised
decisions.reason: Readable turns the noun into a verb, which is easier to follow.

records.source: σπείρεται ἐν φθορᾷ, ἐγείρεται ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ·
records.gloss: It is sown in decay, it is raised in imperishability;
pieces: It is sown in decay; it is raised imperishable.

L.42: It is sown in decay; it is raised in imperishability.

R.42: The body is put in the ground like a seed, and it decays. But it will be raised, and then it can never decay.

decisions.choice: it is sown: the body is buried in death, like a seed put in the ground
alternatives: the body is "sown" at birth and through the whole of this life
decisions.reason: The subject is not named; it is the body (verses 35, 44). The picture of the seed that must die (verse 36) suggests that sowing means burial. Some take it to mean the whole present life, which is already marked by decay and weakness; verse 44, "it is sown a natural body", can be read either way.

decisions.choice: decay: being subject to decay and death; imperishability: being beyond decay
decisions.reason: φθορᾷ means decay or ruin, what happens to every living body. ἀφθαρσίᾳ is the opposite, what cannot decay (Romans 2:7; 2 Timothy 1:10). Paul is speaking of the body, not of sin.

decisions.choice: present tenses: what always happens, said of the resurrection as a sure thing
decisions.reason: Like the farmer's sowing (verses 36-37), the four pairs in verses 42-44 state what is true of every believer who dies and is raised.

decisions.choice: The body is put in the ground like a seed; it will be raised; it can never decay
alternatives: it is sown in decay, raised in imperishability
decisions.reason: Readable names the body, explains the picture of sowing (m1, which is uncertain) and uses verbs instead of the nouns. The future "will be" says what the present tense means here (m3).

records.source: σπείρεται ἐν ἀτιμίᾳ, ἐγείρεται ἐν δόξῃ· σπείρεται ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ, ἐγείρεται ἐν δυνάμει·
records.gloss: It is sown in dishonor, it is raised in glory; it is sown in weakness, it is raised in power;
pieces: In dishonor it is sown, in glory it is raised; in weakness it is sown, in power it is raised.

L.43: It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power.

R.43: When it is buried, it has no honor, but it will be raised in glory. When it is buried, it is weak, but it will be raised with power.

decisions.choice: dishonor: the shame and helplessness of death; glory: the splendor of the raised body
decisions.reason: ἀτιμίᾳ is lack of honor, the humiliation of a body that dies and is buried. δόξῃ is the glory of verses 40-41; Paul says the raised body will be like Christ's body of glory (Philippians 3:21).

decisions.choice: weakness: the frailty of the mortal body; power: the strength God gives in the resurrection
decisions.reason: ἀσθενείᾳ is the frailty of bodies that tire, fall ill and die. δυνάμει is the power of God that raised Christ (6:14; 2 Corinthians 13:4).

decisions.choice: When it is buried (R)
decisions.reason: Readable explains sowing as burial, following 42.s2 m1, which is uncertain.

decisions.choice: In dishonor it is sown, in glory it is raised (B)
alternatives: It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory
decisions.reason: Balanced puts the contrasting nouns first, where the stress falls when the verse is read aloud; the Greek sets them against each other at the end of each clause.

records.source: σπείρεται σῶμα ψυχικόν, ἐγείρεται σῶμα πνευματικόν.
records.gloss: It is sown a body natural, it is raised a body spiritual.
pieces: What is sown is a natural body; what is raised is a spiritual body.

L.44: It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body.

R.44: The body that is buried has ordinary human life. The body that is raised will be given life by God's Spirit.

decisions.choice: natural body: a body with ordinary human life, as people have it by nature
decisions.reason: ψυχικόν is the word of 2:14, built on ψυχὴν ("life, living being"), which verse 45 quotes from Genesis 2:7. It describes the body with the life Adam received at creation, the life every human being has. It is weak and mortal, but it is not evil.

decisions.choice: spiritual body: a body given life and ruled by the Spirit of God, not a body made of spirit
alternatives: a body made of a fine, heavenly substance
a body that is not physical
decisions.reason: Paul's adjectives of this kind say what something is marked by, not what it is made of: the "spiritual" person of 2:15 has God's Spirit, and the "spiritual" food and drink of 10:3-4 were real food and water given by God. The raised body is still a body; it is made alive by the Spirit, who already gives life to mortal bodies (Romans 8:11). Some read the word as describing a body made of spirit rather than flesh.

decisions.choice: natural body, spiritual body (L, B)
alternatives: a body with only natural life
decisions.reason: "Physical body" would suggest that the raised body is not physical, which m2 does not accept. In 2:14 Balanced says "a person who has only natural life"; here, set against "spiritual body" and taken up again in verse 46, "natural body" is clear.

decisions.choice: has ordinary human life; will be given life by God's Spirit
decisions.reason: Readable says what the two kinds of body are (m1, m2), as 2:14 does for the natural person.

records.source: Εἰ ἔστιν σῶμα ψυχικόν, ἔστιν καὶ πνευματικόν.
records.gloss: If there is a body natural, there is also spiritual.
pieces: If a natural body exists, a spiritual body exists too.

L.44: If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual [one].

R.44: There is a body with ordinary human life, and so there is also a body given life by the Spirit.

decisions.choice: if: a real condition; since the one exists, so does the other
decisions.reason: Εἰ with the present states something both sides grant: there are natural bodies. Paul argues that there is also a spiritual body, and grounds it at once in Scripture (verse 45).

decisions.choice: and so (R)
decisions.reason: Readable states the condition as a fact, since it is one (m1).

records.source: οὕτως καὶ γέγραπται· Ἐγένετο ὁ πρῶτος ἄνθρωπος Ἀδὰμ εἰς ψυχὴν ζῶσαν· ὁ ἔσχατος Ἀδὰμ εἰς πνεῦμα ζῳοποιοῦν.
records.gloss: So also it has been written: Became the first man Adam into a being living; the last Adam into a spirit life-giving.
pieces: This is also what Scripture says: "Adam, the first man, became a living being." The last Adam became a spirit who gives life.

L.45: So also it is written, "The first man Adam became a living being"; the last Adam [became] a life-giving spirit.

R.45: Scripture says, "Adam, the first man, became a living being." But Christ, the last Adam, became a spirit who gives life.

decisions.choice: Genesis 2:7, with "first" and "Adam" added
alternatives: the whole verse as a quotation
decisions.reason: Genesis 2:7 says that God breathed into the man the breath of life and the man became a living being. Paul adds πρῶτος ("first") and Ἀδὰμ ("Adam"). The second half of the verse, about the last Adam, is not in Genesis; it is Paul's own statement, set beside the quotation.

decisions.choice: a living being: a creature with natural life
alternatives: a soul as the inner part of a person
decisions.reason: ψυχὴν with "living" is a living creature. The word is the root of ψυχικόν ("natural") in verse 44: the natural body is the body Adam received at creation, before he sinned.

decisions.choice: the last Adam: Christ, the head of a new humanity
decisions.reason: As in verses 21-22 and Romans 5:14, Adam and Christ each stand at the head of a humanity. Christ is the "last" Adam because no other will follow. He became a life-giving spirit at his resurrection (Romans 1:4), when he began the life the raised will share.

decisions.choice: a life-giving spirit: the risen Christ, who gives the life of the Spirit
decisions.reason: πνεῦμα stands opposite ψυχὴν: Adam received life, Christ gives it. The risen Christ gives life by the Spirit (Romans 8:9-11; 2 Corinthians 3:17). Paul does not mean that Christ turned into the Holy Spirit, nor that he has no body; his point is the kind of life he has and gives. Some print "Spirit" with a capital, to show the link to the Holy Spirit.

decisions.choice: living being
decisions.reason: In English "soul" suggests the inner, non-bodily part of a person, which is not the sense (m2).

decisions.choice: spirit, lowercase
decisions.reason: The lowercase keeps the parallel with "living being" and avoids making Christ the same as the Holy Spirit (m4).

decisions.choice: But Christ, the last Adam (R)
decisions.reason: Readable names Christ (m3).

decisions.choice: Adam, the first man (B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the name first, so that "the first man" reads as a description that prepares for "the last Adam".

records.source: ἀλλ’ οὐ πρῶτον τὸ πνευματικὸν ἀλλὰ τὸ ψυχικόν, ἔπειτα τὸ πνευματικόν.
records.gloss: But not first the spiritual but the natural, then the spiritual.
pieces: The spiritual does not come first. The natural comes first, and the spiritual after it.

L.46: But the spiritual [is] not first, but the natural, then the spiritual.

R.46: The body with ordinary human life comes first. The body given life by the Spirit comes later.

decisions.choice: the spiritual, the natural: the two kinds of body of verse 44
alternatives: a general rule about spiritual things
decisions.reason: The neuter adjectives take up "natural body" and "spiritual body" from verse 44. Adam's body came first; the body like the risen Christ's comes after.

decisions.choice: the order is God's plan in history: first creation, then resurrection
alternatives: Paul is correcting a teaching that a heavenly, spiritual man came first
decisions.reason: Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish writer of Paul's time, read Genesis 1 and 2 as speaking of two men, a heavenly one made first and an earthly one made later. Paul may be answering such an idea, or he may simply be stating the order of God's work. Either way, the spiritual body belongs to the future, not to the present.

decisions.choice: The body with ordinary human life; the body given life by the Spirit (R)
decisions.reason: Readable names the two bodies, as in verse 44 (m1).

records.source: ὁ πρῶτος ἄνθρωπος ἐκ γῆς χοϊκός, ὁ δεύτερος ἄνθρωπος ἐξ οὐρανοῦ.
records.gloss: The first man from earth, of dust; the second man from heaven.
pieces: The first man came from the earth and was made of dust; the second man comes from heaven.

L.47: The first man [was] from [the] earth, made of dust; the second man [is] from heaven.

R.47: The first man, Adam, was made from the dust of the ground. The second man, Christ, came from heaven.

decisions.choice: from the earth, made of dust: Adam formed from the ground
decisions.reason: Genesis 2:7 says God formed the man from the dust of the ground; Genesis 3:19 adds that to dust he will return. χοϊκός means "made of dust".

decisions.choice: from heaven: the risen Christ, whose origin and life are heavenly
alternatives: only Christ's coming into the world as a man
decisions.reason: In the setting of the resurrection body, "from heaven" most likely speaks of the risen Christ, who will come from heaven and change our bodies to be like his (Philippians 3:20-21; 1 Thessalonians 4:16). It may also include his coming as a man.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "the second man from heaven"
alternatives: "the second man is the Lord from heaven"
